title: Ten months in a band at 110th Street, then shipped to Kentucky
summary: He lived at home on a daily pass while in the 372nd Infantry's band; when the unit moved to Camp Breckenridge the Colonel had arranged for his place.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: So I was at 110th Street, and I was at 110th Street about 10 months, and it was beautiful, because I played in a band and every day at 5:00 o'clock I'd get what you call your Class A pass, and I'd go home. Yeah.

It was just perfect. But then that was broken up. You know, the Army does a lot of things with no explanation, because there are so many people in the Army who are getting paid, and they have to think up things to do to earn the money. That goes for General Eisenhower down to the Corporal. See, that's why they call the Private a Buck Private, because he has nobody to pass the buck to. So anyway, we were shipped out and we were shipped to Camp Breckenridge, Kentucky, and the same thing down there, we were in this band and we would rehearse, and that was the end of it.

We didn't have to do, you know, any soldiering, in a way of speaking. And this was an infantry regiment, infantry. We who were in the band didn't have anything to do, but it was an unauthorized band, by grace of the Colonel, and we had our own barrack and which was just the Colonel's doing, because the 372nd Infantry was a Boston regiment, was an old National Guard regiment which had battle flags from World War I and the Spanish-American War. And it -- and it was a funny thing, not funny, but the thing was on the parade grounds, when the troops were parading for inspection or whatever, our regiment was the only regiment that had battle flags. The rest of the troops -- and ours was one of the very, very few black outfits in the Army which was black from the Colonel down. There wasn't a white officer in the regiment.

And now, getting back to why I was allowed to come to 110th Street, because this friend of mine who was a private was a friend of the Colonel's. So he just went to the Colonel and told him, "I've got a friend." You know, told him who I was, I was a musician and who I played with, you know, a little background. And the Colonel just said okay, and that was it. So I came to 110th Street. That's how I got there.
